pkg_11_physics_thermodynamics.topic: The Carnot Cycle, Maximum Theoretical Efficiency, and Entropy
pkg_11_physics_thermodynamics.root_concept: Carnot Cycle, Maximum Theoretical Efficiency, and Entropy

concepts.name: Heat engine definition and energy balance (First Law)
concepts.observed_summary: A heat engine is defined as a device that operates in a thermodynamic cycle, absorbs heat Q_H from a high‑temperature reservoir at T_H, does net work W, and rejects heat Q_C to a low‑temperature reservoir at T_C; the First Law gives W = Q_H – Q_C and the thermal efficiency η = W/Q_H = 1 – Q_C/Q_H.

evidence_quotes.quote: Recall that a heat engine is any device that operates in a thermodynamic cycle, absorbs heat Q_H from a high-temperature thermal reservoir at T_H, converts a fraction of this thermal energy into net mechanical work W, and rejects the remaining heat Q_C to a low-temperature reservoir at T_C. By the First Law of Thermodynamics, energy is conserved, so net work output is W equals Q_H minus Q_C.
The thermal efficiency of any heat engine is defined as the desired output divided by the required energy input, which is eta equals W over Q_H, or 1 minus Q_C over Q_H.

concepts.name: Carnot cycle as the reversible benchmark
concepts.observed_summary: The Carnot cycle is introduced as the theoretical reversible engine that sets the maximum possible efficiency for any engine operating between two temperatures, as established by Sadi Carnot in 1824.

evidence_quotes.quote: In 1824, French engineer Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot established that no heat engine operating between two given temperatures can be more efficient than a reversible engine operating between the same two temperatures. This theoretical ideal is known as the Carnot cycle.

concepts.name: Four reversible processes of the Carnot cycle for an ideal gas
concepts.observed_summary: The lecture enumerates the four reversible steps: (1) isothermal expansion at T_H (heat absorbed Q_H = nRT_H ln(V2/V1)), (2) adiabatic expansion (temperature drops from T_H to T_C), (3) isothermal compression at T_C (heat rejected Q_C = nRT_C ln(V3/V4)), and (4) adiabatic compression (temperature rises back to T_H).

evidence_quotes.quote: Process 1 to 2 is Reversible Isothermal Expansion... The gas expands slowly from volume V1 to V2 while absorbing heat Q_H... Q_H equals n times R times T_H times natural log of V2 over V1.
Process 2 to 3 is Reversible Adiabatic Expansion... the working fluid temperature drops from the source temperature T_H down to the sink temperature T_C.
Process 3 to 4 is Reversible Isothermal Compression... The magnitude of heat rejected is Q_C equals n times R times T_C times natural log of V3 over V4.
Process 4 to 1 is Reversible Adiabatic Compression... raising its temperature from T_C back up to T_H, completing the closed cycle.

concepts.name: Derivation of the Carnot efficiency η = 1 – T_C/T_H
concepts.observed_summary: Starting from η = 1 – Q_C/Q_H, the isothermal heat expressions are substituted, the nR terms cancel, and the adiabatic relations are used to show V2/V1 = V3/V4, which cancels the logarithmic terms, yielding η_Carnot = 1 – T_C/T_H; the result depends only on reservoir temperatures.

evidence_quotes.quote: We know that eta equals 1 minus Q_C over Q_H. Substituting our isothermal heat expressions... the n and R terms cancel, giving (T_C ln(V3/V4)) over (T_H ln(V2/V1)).

For adiabatic expansion 2 to 3: T_H times V2^(gamma‑1) equals T_C times V3^(gamma‑1). For adiabatic compression 4 to 1: T_H times V1^(gamma‑1) equals T_C times V4^(gamma‑1). Dividing... V2 over V1 equals V3 over V4! Therefore, the logarithmic volume terms ... cancel out completely!
We arrive at the definitive result: eta_Carnot equals 1 minus T_C over T_H.

pkg_12_pharmacology_clearance.topic: One-Compartment Intravenous Pharmacokinetics: Clearance and Half-Life

concepts.name: One-Compartment Open Model
concepts.observed_summary: The lecture introduced the one‑compartment open model, describing the body as a single, well‑mixed kinetic container of volume V_d that receives an IV bolus dose.

evidence_quotes.quote: The simplest model is the One-Compartment Open Model. In this model, the body is treated as a single, well-mixed kinetic container of volume V_d.

concepts.name: Apparent Volume of Distribution (V_d)
concepts.observed_summary: V_d is defined as the proportionality factor relating total drug amount to plasma concentration (V_d = Dose / C_0) and explained as an apparent, not anatomical, volume that can be very large for lipid‑soluble drugs.

evidence_quotes.quote: Apparent Volume of Distribution (V_d): defined as the proportionality factor relating the total amount of drug in the body to the measured plasma concentration: V_d equals Dose divided by C_0. It does not necessarily represent a true anatomical fluid volume...

concepts.name: Elimination Rate Constant (k_e)
concepts.observed_summary: k_e is the fraction of drug removed per unit time, expressed in hr⁻¹, and serves as the slope parameter for first‑order elimination.

evidence_quotes.quote: Elimination Rate Constant (k_e): the fraction of drug removed from the body per unit time, with units of inverse hours (hr^-1).

concepts.name: Total Systemic Clearance (CL) and its relationship CL = k_e·V_d
concepts.observed_summary: Clearance is the volume of plasma cleared per unit time (L/hr). The lecture derived CL = k_e × V_d from the definition of clearance as rate of elimination divided by concentration.

evidence_quotes.quote: Total Systemic Clearance (CL): the volume of blood or plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time... Clearance equals k_e times V_d.

concepts.name: Elimination Half‑Life (t_1/2) and formula t_1/2 = 0.693/k_e
concepts.observed_summary: Half‑life is the time for plasma concentration to fall by 50%; derived mathematically as t_1/2 = 0.693/k_e.

evidence_quotes.quote: Elimination Half-Life (t_1/2): the time required for the plasma concentration to decrease by exactly 50%... t_1/2 equals 0.693 divided by k_e.

concepts.name: First‑order elimination differential equation and exponential decay solution
concepts.observed_summary: Assuming first‑order kinetics, dC/dt = –k_e·C; integration yields C(t) = C_0·e^(–k_e·t).

evidence_quotes.quote: Assuming first-order elimination kinetics, the rate of drug elimination is directly proportional to the amount of drug remaining in the body: dC/dt equals minus k_e times C... Exponentiating both sides yields the classical exponential decay equation: C(t) equals C_0 times e to the power of minus k_e times t.

pkg_13_logic_predicates.topic: First-Order Predicate Logic: Quantifiers, Variable Binding, and Semantics

concepts.name: Non‑logical symbols (individual constants, variables, predicate symbols)
concepts.observed_summary: Introduced constants as lowercase letters denoting specific objects, variables as placeholders ranging over the domain, and predicate symbols for properties and relations.

evidence_quotes.quote: Individual Constants: denote specific individual objects in our domain, written as lowercase letters a, b, c (for example, s for Socrates).
Variables: serve as placeholders that range over objects in the domain, denoted by x, y, z.
Predicate Symbols: represent properties of individuals or relations among individuals. A 1‑place predicate like H(x) means 'x is human'. A 2‑place relation like A(x, y) means 'x admires y'.

concepts.name: Quantifiers (universal and existential)
concepts.observed_summary: Defined the universal quantifier (∀) as ‘for all x’ and the existential quantifier (∃) as ‘there exists at least one x’.

evidence_quotes.quote: Quantifiers: we have two fundamental quantifiers: - The Universal Quantifier, written as upside‑down A, meaning 'for all x' or 'for every x'. - The Existential Quantifier, written as backwards E, meaning 'there exists at least one x' or 'for some x'.

concepts.name: Scope and variable binding (free vs. bound variables)
concepts.observed_summary: Explained how parentheses delimit the scope of a quantifier, how a variable inside that scope is bound, and that variables not bound are free; a formula with no free variables is a closed sentence.

evidence_quotes.quote: Scope and Binding: in the formula forall x (H(x) -> M(x)), the parentheses define the scope of the universal quantifier. The variable x occurring inside H(x) and M(x) is bound by the quantifier. A variable that is not bound by any quantifier is called a free variable. A formula with no free variables is a closed sentence.

concepts.name: Quantifier negation duality
concepts.observed_summary: Stated the logical equivalences ¬∀x H(x) ⇔ ∃x ¬H(x) and ¬∃x H(x) ⇔ ∀x ¬H(x).

evidence_quotes.quote: To say 'Not everyone is happy' is logically equivalent to saying 'There exists someone who is not happy': not forall x H(x) is equivalent to exists x not H(x). Similarly, to say 'No one is happy' is logically equivalent to saying 'For everyone, they are not happy': not exists x H(x) is equivalent to forall x not H(x).

concepts.name: Model‑theoretic semantics (model structure: domain and interpretation)
concepts.observed_summary: Defined a model M = ⟨D, I⟩ where D is a non‑empty domain of objects and I assigns each constant an element of D and each n‑place predicate a set of n‑tuples from D.

evidence_quotes.quote: A Model M is an ordered pair M = <D, I>, where: - D is the Domain of Discourse: a non‑empty set of objects that the logic talks about. - I is the Interpretation Function, which assigns meaning to non‑logical symbols: * To each individual constant c, I(c) is an element of D. * To each n‑place predicate symbol P, I(P) is a set of n‑tuples of elements from D.

concepts.name: Variable assignment and satisfaction conditions for quantifiers
concepts.observed_summary: Introduced a variable assignment g mapping variables to domain elements and gave the truth conditions: M,g ⊨ ∀x φ iff for every d∈D, M,g[x↦d] ⊨ φ; and M,g ⊨ ∃x φ iff there exists d∈D such that M,g[x↦d] ⊨ φ.

evidence_quotes.quote: The formal satisfaction condition states: M, g satisfies forall x phi if and only if for every element d in D, M with assignment g modified so x maps to d satisfies phi. M, g satisfies exists x phi if and only if there exists at least one element d in D such that M with assignment g modified so x maps to d satisfies phi.

concepts.name: Worked example: translation and model evaluation of a quantified sentence
concepts.observed_summary: Translated ‘Every philosopher admires some logician’ as ∀x(P(x) → ∃y(L(y) ∧ A(x,y))) and evaluated it in a concrete model with domain {p1,l1,l2}, showing the sentence is true because p1 (the only philosopher) admires l1 (a logician).

evidence_quotes.quote: Suppose our English sentence is: 'Every philosopher admires some logician.' ... The correct translation requires nested quantifiers: forall x (P(x) -> exists y (L(y) and A(x, y))). ... Let Domain D = {p1, l1, l2}. ... Does M satisfy the sentence? ... Therefore, the sentence evaluates to TRUE in this model M.

concepts.name: Quantifier inference rules (Universal Instantiation and Existential Generalization)
concepts.observed_summary: Stated the two standard quantifier rules: UI allows inference from ∀x φ to φ[c/x]; EG allows inference from φ[c] to ∃x φ.

evidence_quotes.quote: The standard deductive system has two quantifier rules: 1. Universal Instantiation (UI): from forall x phi, you may infer phi with variable x replaced by any constant c, written phi[c/x]. 2. Existential Generalization (EG): from phi[c], you may infer exists x phi.

concepts.name: Boundary case: empty domains and free logic
concepts.observed_summary: Noted that standard Tarskian semantics require a non‑empty domain; if the domain were empty, ∀x P(x) would be vacuously true and ∃x P(x) false, leading to free‑logic systems that relax this requirement.

evidence_quotes.quote: In standard Tarskian logic, the domain D is axiomatically required to be non‑empty. If D were empty, forall x P(x) would be vacuously true while exists x P(x) would be false, violating standard existential entailment. Systems that handle empty domains are called Free Logics...

pkg_14_signal_processing_fourier.topic: Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) and Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem
pkg_14_signal_processing_fourier.root_concept: Discrete Fourier Transform and Nyquist‑Shannon Sampling Theorem

concepts.name: Continuous‑to‑discrete signal conversion (sampling)
concepts.observed_summary: The lecture defined how a continuous‑time signal x(t) is turned into a discrete‑time sequence x[n] by sampling at uniform intervals T_s, with x[n] = x(n T_s).

evidence_quotes.quote: We convert continuous signals to discrete sequences x[n] by sampling at uniform time intervals T_s, where sampling frequency f_s equals 1 over T_s, such that x[n] = x(n T_s).

concepts.name: Sampling parameters: interval T_s and frequency f_s
concepts.observed_summary: The instructor identified the sampling interval T_s and its reciprocal sampling frequency f_s = 1/T_s as the fundamental parameters governing the discrete representation.

evidence_quotes.quote: sampling at uniform time intervals T_s, where sampling frequency f_s equals 1 over T_s

concepts.name: Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) definition
concepts.observed_summary: The DFT was introduced as the tool to analyse the frequency content of a finite discrete sequence of length N, with the analysis equation X[k] = Σ_{n=0}^{N‑1} x[n]·e^{‑j2πkn/N}.

evidence_quotes.quote: To analyze the frequency content of a finite discrete sequence of length N, we use the Discrete Fourier Transform, or DFT. The DFT Analysis Equation transforms N time-domain samples x[0] through x[N-1] into N frequency-domain coefficients X[0] through X[N-1]: X[k] equals the summation from n equals 0 to N minus 1 of x[n] times e to the power of minus j times 2 pi times k times n divided by N, for k = 0, 1 up to N-1.

concepts.name: Twiddle factor notation W_N^{kn}
concepts.observed_summary: The exponential term e^{‑j2πkn/N} was identified as the twiddle factor, denoted W_N^{kn}.

evidence_quotes.quote: The term e^(-j 2 pi k n / N) is often denoted as the twiddle factor W_N^(k n).

concepts.name: Frequency‑bin mapping and spectral resolution
concepts.observed_summary: The relationship between DFT index k and physical frequency was given as f_k = k·f_s/N, and the spacing Δf = f_s/N was defined as the spectral resolution, which improves with larger N.

evidence_quotes.quote: What frequency does index k actually correspond to in Hertz? The frequency of bin k is given by f_k equals k times f_s divided by N. The spacing between adjacent frequency bins is Delta f equals f_s divided by N, which is called the Spectral Resolution of the DFT.

concepts.name: Worked 4‑point DFT example
concepts.observed_summary: A concrete calculation for N=4 with input x=[1,2,0,‑1] was performed, showing X[0]=2 and X[1]=1‑3j with magnitude √10 ≈ 3.16.

evidence_quotes.quote: Let us trace a worked numerical calculation for an N = 4 point DFT. Suppose our discrete input sequence is x = [1, 2, 0, -1]... For k = 0 (the DC component): X[0] equals ... 2. For k = 1: X[1] equals ... 1 - 3j! The magnitude is |X[1]| = sqrt(1^2 + (-3)^2) = sqrt(10) approx 3.16.

concepts.name: Nyquist‑Shannon Sampling Theorem statement
concepts.observed_summary: The theorem was stated: to avoid aliasing the sampling rate must satisfy f_s > 2 f_max, with f_Nyquist = f_s/2 as the Nyquist (folding) frequency.

evidence_quotes.quote: Now, let us examine the fundamental limit of sampling: the Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem... To avoid aliasing, the sampling rate must strictly satisfy the Nyquist Criterion: f_s must be strictly greater than twice the highest frequency present in the signal: f_s > 2 * f_max.

concepts.name: Aliasing and its spectral‑replica explanation
concepts.observed_summary: Aliasing was described as the overlap of spectral replicas when signal components exceed f_s/2, causing higher frequencies to fold back into the baseband and become indistinguishable from low‑frequency content.

evidence_quotes.quote: If the continuous signal contains frequencies higher than half the sampling rate, these spectral replicas overlap. This catastrophic distortion is called Aliasing. Frequencies higher than f_s / 2 fold back into the lower frequency spectrum and become indistinguishable from genuine low-frequency signals.
